title: Marn and the Missing Wobble
markdown:
The wind on the high ridges tickled ears and made hair dance. Clouds brushed the peaks. Below, the ridge-woven land lay like a misty blanket stitched with rock, monasteries clinging to cliffsides like wise old birds, meadows inviting a wanderer to forget the time.

Marn the ogre moved through that country as the earth itself might move if it had decided to be kind. He was strong as a mountain and almost as patient. His constant shadow was Ink, a cat black as night, sleek as polished obsidian, with emerald eyes that held the twilight’s secrets. Ink did not meow much. When she did, it meant something.

The problem, when it arrived, was perfectly sensible. The bridge that carried extra-fluffy cloud-wool across Whisperwind Gorge had developed a wobble. Not a crash-and-bang wobble. A little shimmy when the wind blew just so. Marn had a plan involving good strong wood and sturdy rope. He had his tools ready, even his favourite chisel, which was as big and blunt as a tree stump.

The people of Whispering Heights loved stories more than instructions. When Marn mentioned the wobble, they did not think of loose planks. They thought of the Grumble-Gloom Beast: a vast damp-socked thing said to live in the gorge, whose grumbles shook slate, whose breath smelled of sour moonberries and wet wool, and whose temper turned foul if anyone looked too closely at the timber it claimed as its own. The taboo was simple and strictly kept. You did not treat a gorge-trouble as carpentry. You appeased.

“You can’t just fix a bridge, Marn,” exclaimed Elara, a weaver with magpie-bright eyes and a voice that could untangle any thread. “You must offer it a song of the seven sorrows, or maybe some fermented moonberries.” She waved her hands and nearly tipped a basket of very round pebbles.

Marn blinked. His large gentle hands held a spool of the finest rope. He looked at the rope, then at Elara, then back at the rope. “The bridge,” he rumbled, as low and pleasant as a bumblebee in a huge flower, “has a loose plank. I have planks.” He held up a smooth piece of seasoned oak.

The idea of a beast was far more exciting than a rotten plank. A crowd gathered with ancient scrolls and very little common sense, reciting verses that sounded like a recipe for sour jam mixed with complaints about the price of cloud-wool. Marn sighed, a soft sound like wind through a hollow log. Arguing about mythical creatures went in circles, much like the wind in the gorge.

That was the first impossible task: to stand still while the song of seven sorrows was offered to a beast that had never asked for it, and to answer with kindness instead of contempt. Marn did not mock them. He waited. Ink sat on his boot and washed a paw, which was her way of saying the verses would not nail a plank.

Then a new complication arrived. Faelar the elf cartographer, whom most people only saw in elaborate tapestries, appeared with hair the colour of moonlight and clothes embroidered with tiny perfect constellations. He carried a measuring tape long enough to stretch across a small kingdom. He was not interested in beasts or bridges. He saw the world as a giant puzzle that needed to be measured and catalogued.

“Halt,” said Faelar, like the clear chime of tiny icicles. “We cannot possibly assess the bridge’s structural integrity without a thorough survey of the gorge’s wind currents and the ground beneath its foundations.” He unfurled the tape. It unspooled with surprising speed down the cliff, narrowly missing a flock of startled mountain goats, gleamed in the sun, and vanished into swirling mist.

That was the second impossible task: to let the gorge swallow a kingdom’s length of tape without chasing it, and still keep hold of a practical plan. Marn watched the tape disappear. He felt sturdy. He felt decent. He also felt a growing urge to get on with the work so the monks might have their wool. Faelar muttered about angles and momentum. The villagers debated the Grumble-Gloom’s taste in cheese.

Ink showed her quiet brilliance then. While Marn patiently tried to explain that a wobble was not a geological anomaly requiring spectral analysis, she padded towards the gorge’s edge without a sound. She sniffed the air with her tiny pink nose, then hopped onto a narrow ledge Faelar’s tape had missed.

Snow from the night before still dusted the highest peaks. Against that white, Ink’s footprints were the most perfect little crosses, a tiny trail leading to a particularly wobbly section of the bridge. She walked with delicate certainty, tested the beam, flicked her tail, and returned to Marn. She sat, looking up at him, then at the problem plank. It was a silent report.

That was the third impossible task: to follow a cat’s path a grown ogre could not take, and to trust what small paws had found. Marn looked at Ink, then at the tiny footprints. A slow knowing smile spread across his face. It was not a beast. It was not shifting earth. It was one weak spot, a compromised timber a small agile creature could navigate, and which was dangerously unstable for anything heavier.

“Faelar,” Marn said, clear and strong, “the problem is here.” He pointed to the spot Ink had shown him. “It is not a beast. It is a rotten beam. Ink found it.”

Faelar, who had been trying to measure the speed of a falling pebble with a contraption of feathers and wind, blinked. His moonlight hair seemed to lose a little of its sparkle. “A cat?” he whispered.

“A very clever cat,” Marn agreed. With surprising speed he took a sturdy piece of timber and a strong length of rope from his supplies. Guided by Ink’s silent watch, her tail occasionally twitching in approval, he reinforced the beam. The wobble vanished. The bridge felt solid, dependable, ready for cloud-wool.

The Grumble-Gloom, if it had ever been more than damp socks and a good story, showed its true form in that single colourful moment: not a monster in the mist, but a length of timber gone brown at the heart, smelling faintly of wet wool and old rain, the very thing the taboo had forbidden anyone to look at properly.

Just as Marn finished, a vast iridescent shadow fell over them. A dragon, scales like polished obsidian, wings a living rainbow, circled once without roar or fire, leaving the faint scent of ozone and distant thunder.

“Dragons,” Marn sighed, watching it climb, “always arrive as if they’ve been invited by the weather.”

The villagers, hushed by that majesty, looked at the solid bridge, then at Marn, then at Ink, who was calmly grooming a paw. The legends seemed a little less important. Faelar packed away what remained of his measuring pride and promised to include feline-based structural diagnostics in future surveys. He even sketched a tiny approving Ink into his notebook. Elara, humbled without being shamed, offered Marn a cup of surprisingly good cloud-berry tea, its sweetness a welcome change from sour pronouncements.

As the sun dipped and painted the ridges rose and gold, Marn stroked Ink. “You know, Ink,” he murmured, “sometimes the most sensible plan needs a little purr-suasion.” Ink answered with a soft rumbling motor of contentment. The cloud-wool would cross. The monks would be warm. The companion who had kept the secret of the ledge had been constant, and constancy, it turned out, was a better spell than any song of seven sorrows.
characters: Marn (good-hearted ogre of the ridge-woven land), Ink (a sleek black cat with emerald eyes)
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, amusing fantasy story for older readers
